symptoms: Dark circular spots appear on leaves, starting from lower leaves. Concentric ring-like patterns. Yellowing around affected areas. Spots may appear on stems and fruits.
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani. Spreads through spores in wet conditions.
favorable_conditions: High humidity, wet leaves, warm temperatures (68-77°F), poor air circulation
management: Remove severely infected leaves. Improve air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Maintain proper spacing between plants. Apply fungicide if needed.
prevention: Crop rotation (2-3 years). Use disease-free seeds. Avoid working in wet fields. Remove infected plant debris. Proper spacing for air circulation.
treatment: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb fungicides. Copper-based fungicides. Apply at first sign of disease.
keywords: early blight, spot, alternaria, fungal, leaf spot

symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves with white mold on undersides. Brown spots on stems and fruits. Leaves may wilt and collapse. Entire plant can be destroyed in severe cases.
causes: Phytophthora infestans fungus. Spreads rapidly in cool, wet weather.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60-75°F), high humidity, leaf wetness for 12+ hours
management: Remove infected plant parts immediately. Improve drainage. Avoid overhead watering. Apply fungicides preventively. Remove plants if severely affected.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Crop rotation (3 years). Good drainage. Avoid waterlogging. Monitor weather conditions. Preventive fungicide spraying.
treatment: Metalaxyl or Mancozeb fungicides. Start treatment early. Spray every 7-10 days in favorable conditions.
keywords: late blight, phytophthora, fungal, wet, rain

symptoms: Small circular spots (1/8 inch diameter) with gray center and dark brown margin. Black dots (pycnidia) visible in center. Yellow halo around spots. Spots merge and leaves dry out.
causes: Septoria lycopersici fungus. Spreads through water splash and contaminated tools.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (68-86°F), high humidity, wet foliage
management: Remove lower infected leaves. Avoid overhead irrigation. Prune to improve air circulation. Disinfect tools. Apply fungicides.
prevention: Use disease-free seeds. Crop rotation (2-3 years). Avoid overhead watering. Proper spacing. Remove infected debris.
treatment: Chlorothalonil, Maneb, or Copper fungicides. Spray every 7-10 days starting early.

symptoms: Leaf blast: Diamond-shaped grayish-brown lesions with reddish-brown borders on leaves. Panicle blast: Gray-brown lesions on neck, rachis causing sterility. Nodal blast affects tillers.
causes: Magnaporthe oryzae fungus. Spores spread by wind and water. High nitrogen increases susceptibility.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (68-77°F), high humidity, dense planting, high nitrogen fertilization
management: Reduce nitrogen fertilizer. Improve drainage. Avoid dense planting. Apply fungicides. Use resistant varieties. Adjust planting dates.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Balanced fertilization. Proper spacing. Adequate drainage. Avoid excessive nitrogen. Use certified seeds.
treatment: Tricyclazole fungicide. Spray at boot stage or panicle initiation stage. Repeat every 14 days if needed.

symptoms: Small brown circular or oval lesions on leaves with yellow or reddish halo. Center may have gray appearance. Lesions coalesce on severely infected leaves.
causes: Cochliobolus miyabeanus fungus. Often associated with poor soil conditions and low nutrients.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures, high humidity, low potassium in soil
management: Improve soil fertility especially potassium. Drain excess water. Apply fungicides. Remove infected plant material.
prevention: Balanced fertilization especially potassium. Good drainage. Use resistant varieties. Use certified seeds. Clean seed treatment.
treatment: Mancozeb or Copper-based fungicides. Spray every 10-14 days starting from early growth stages.
keywords: brown spot, rice, fungal, leaf disease

symptoms: Leaves: Water-soaked lesions with white mold on leaf undersides. Lesions have irregular borders. Tubers: Dark, sunken rot. Infected tubers have firm gray-brown rot inside.
causes: Cool, wet conditions favor the disease. Spores spread by wind and water.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60-75°F), high humidity, rain, leaf wetness for 12+ hours
management: Remove infected plant parts. Improve drainage. Avoid overhead watering. Hoe up plants early. Destroy infected tubers.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Certified seed tubers. Crop rotation (3 years). Avoid overhead watering. Proper drainage. Remove volunteers.
treatment: Metalaxyl, Chlorothalonil, or Mancozeb fungicides. Start treatment early in season. Spray every 7-10 days.
keywords: late blight, potato, fungal, tuber rot

symptoms: Concentric rings (target-like appearance) on older leaves. Brown spots with yellow halo. Spots enlarge and entire leaf may die. Stems may also be affected.
causes: Alternaria solani fungus. Spreads through spores in moist conditions.
favorable_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures, high humidity, poor air circulation
management: Remove lower infected leaves. Improve air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Apply fungicides. Remove dead plant material.
prevention: Crop rotation (3 years). Use disease-free seed. Proper spacing. Avoid overhead watering. Remove volunteers. Use fungicide.
treatment: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Copper fungicides. Start at first sign of disease. Spray every 7-10 days.
keywords: early blight, alternaria, potato, leaf spot

symptoms: Circular brown lesions on fruits, leaves, and stems. Lesions have concentric rings. Center may have black dots (acervuli). Affected fruits become unusable.
causes: Colletotrichum fungus. Spreads through water splash and contaminated tools. High humidity promotes disease.
management: Remove infected fruits immediately. Improve air circulation. Avoid overhead watering. Apply fungicides. Prune lower branches.
prevention: Crop rotation. Use disease-free seeds. Proper spacing for air circulation. Avoid overhead watering. Disinfect tools. Use resistant varieties.
treatment: Carbendazim or Tricyclazole fungicides. Spray every 10-14 days starting from flowering stage.

symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves, stems, and fruits. Leaves may turn yellow and drop. Severely infected plants are weakened. Fruits may have reduced quality.
causes: Leveillula taurica fungus. Spreads through spores in dry conditions.
favorable_conditions: Warm days (75-85°F), cool nights, high humidity, poor air circulation
management: Remove infected leaves. Improve air circulation. Reduce shade. Spray sulfur-based fungicides. Avoid overhead watering.
prevention: Proper spacing for air circulation. Regular pruning. Avoid over-shading. Use resistant varieties. Sulfur application for prevention.
treatment: Sulfur powder or Wettable Sulfur spray. Triadimefon fungicide. Spray every 10-14 days as needed.
keywords: powdery mildew, chilli, fungal, white powder

symptoms: Rusty brown pustules on leaves that break epidermis. Leaves may appear orange-red in severe cases. Pustules are scattered on leaf surface. Stem rust can girdle stems.
causes: Puccinia fungus. Wind-borne spores. Alternate hosts: berberis species (for stem rust).
favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures, high humidity, wind for spore dispersal
management: Timely fungicide application. Use resistant varieties. Ensure proper spacing. Remove alternate hosts.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Timely sowing. Avoid alternate host plants nearby. Proper crop rotation.
treatment: Propiconazole or Mancozeb fungicides. Spray at first sign of pustules. Repeat every 10-14 days if needed.

symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves, stems. Leaves may turn brownish. Severely infected plants have reduced grain fill.
causes: Blumeria graminis fungus. Spreads through spores in cool, dry conditions.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60-75°F), low humidity, poor air circulation, overcrowding
management: Avoid excessive nitrogen. Improve air circulation. Apply fungicides. Use resistant varieties.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Balanced fertilization. Proper spacing. Adequate moisture. Avoid overcrowding.
treatment: Sulfur or Carbendazim fungicides. Spray at first sign of disease. Repeat every 10-14 days.

symptoms: Black or brown lesions on leaves, fruits, and twigs. Lesions have concentric rings. Affected fruits develop dark rot. Flowers may be infected causing panicle blight.
causes: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides fungus. Spreads through spores in wet conditions.
favorable_conditions: Warm, wet weather, high humidity, poor air circulation
management: Prune affected branches. Improve air circulation. Remove fallen leaves. Apply fungicides. Harvest ripe fruits promptly.
prevention: Use fungicide on flowers at panicle stage. Prune overlapping branches. Ensure good drainage. Timely harvesting.
treatment: Carbendazim or Copper fungicides. Spray at flowering and fruit development stages. Repeat every 14-21 days.

symptoms: White powdery coating on young leaves, flowers, and young fruits. Affected parts may not expand properly. Severe infection reduces fruit set.
causes: Oidium mangiferae fungus. Spreads through spores in cool, dry conditions.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (60-80°F), low humidity, mild wind
management: Prune affected parts. Improve air circulation. Spray sulfur fungicides. Remove infected flowers.
prevention: Proper pruning for air circulation. Avoid excessive shade. Use resistant varieties. Sulfur spray for prevention.
treatment: Sulfur powder or Wettable Sulfur. Spray at first sign of disease. Repeat every 15-21 days.

symptoms: Circular brown to black lesions develop on leaves and fruit. Fruit may develop sunken black rot and concentric rings. Dead twigs may show cankers.
causes: Botryosphaeria obtusa. The pathogen survives in dead wood, mummified fruit and cankers and spreads by spores.
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather, prolonged leaf wetness, dead or injured plant tissue
management: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood. Prune cankers during dry weather. Improve orchard sanitation and air circulation. Use locally approved fungicides when required.
prevention: Remove dead wood and mummified fruit. Prune infected branches. Avoid tree injury. Maintain orchard sanitation and balanced tree vigor.
treatment: Use an apple fungicide program appropriate for local agricultural recommendations and label directions.
keywords: black rot, apple, botryosphaeria, fruit rot, canker

symptoms: Leaves and fruit show normal healthy growth without characteristic disease lesions or abnormal discoloration.
causes: No disease detected from the model class.
management: Continue routine orchard monitoring and good crop management.
prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation, balanced nutrition, appropriate irrigation and regular monitoring.

symptoms: Yellow-orange spots may develop on leaves, sometimes with darker margins and orange spore structures. Severe infection can cause premature leaf drop.
causes: Gymnosporangium species; some species require alternate host plants to complete their life cycle.
favorable_conditions: Moist conditions and prolonged leaf wetness during susceptible growth stages
management: Remove affected plant material where practical. Improve orchard sanitation and follow locally recommended fungicide programs.
prevention: Use appropriate resistant cultivars where available. Remove relevant alternate hosts where agronomically and legally appropriate. Maintain orchard sanitation.
treatment: Use only locally approved fungicides according to the product label and agricultural recommendations.

symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety lesions develop on leaves and fruit. Older lesions may become darker and corky; severe infection can cause leaf and fruit drop.
causes: Venturia inaequalis. Spores released from infected fallen leaves spread infection during wet periods.
favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures, high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness
management: Remove fallen infected leaves where practical. Improve canopy airflow. Follow a locally recommended scab-management program.
prevention: Orchard sanitation, resistant varieties where available, good pruning and timely monitoring of wet-weather infection periods.
treatment: Use locally approved fungicides according to label directions and regional agricultural recommendations.
